title: Numerics: the mismatch between the rollout engine and the trainer
design_ref: Numerics and MoE: the mismatch that grows with scale
purpose: Score the same sampled answers with the rollout engine and with the trainer's own forward pass, under four precisions, and look at the shape of the log-ratio between them. Then read the same quantity from a real run's logs.

checks.description: the engine and the trainer disagree even at the same weights and the same precision
checks.because: Different kernels, different reduction orders, a different attention implementation. The log-ratio between the two engines is never exactly zero, even for a small dense model in bf16 on both sides.

checks.description: the tail, not the mean, carries the mismatch: one percent of the tokens hold a large share of it
checks.because: If the mismatch were spread evenly, one percent of the tokens would hold one percent of it. This is why the design watches the fraction of tokens beyond a ratio threshold and not the average, which is tiny.
FP8 weights round every parameter. The engine still samples from a very similar distribution, but the trainer's probabilities for the sampled tokens differ more.

checks.description: a float32 trainer is closer to the engine's probabilities than a bf16 one, or no further
checks.because: The design's published finding is that the final projection to logits in FP32 shifts the ceiling, not only stability. This probe measures the distance, not the ceiling.

checks.description: the truncated importance weight bounds the tokens beyond the cap
checks.because: A weight of min(ratio, cap) keeps one token from dominating a gradient. The share of tokens that hit the cap is the cost.

checks.description: the trainer logs the ratio's distribution on every step of every run
checks.because: The trainer uses the sampler's own probabilities as the old policy, so the importance ratio it already computes covers mismatch and staleness together (see TRL's async trainer).
